new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: exists (23-page image-only extract of the archive.org DLI scan in.ernet.dli.2015.106026, no text layer). I rendered p. 1 (journal p. 293, header 'The Carib Language as now spoken in Dominica, West Indies. By Joseph Numa Rat, St. Kitts, West Indies, February, 1897', section 'Orthography') to PNG and read it: the two quoted sentences are there verbatim, in two consecutive paragraphs -- 'The accent in the Carib words will be indicated by placing the French acute accent over the vowel on which it falls; e.g., in mútu, the accent should be placed on the penultimate, and, in háruti, on the antepenultimate syllable.' / 'As a rule to which I remember no exception, the accent in words of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is antepenultimate in words of three or more syllables and penultimate (= initial) in disyllables, i.e. a right-edge antepenult rule; the author (a St. Kitts physician recording the last Dominican speakers/rememberers in the 1890s) reports no exceptions and marks the accent with an acute on every cited form.
new_statements.exceptions: None ('a rule to which I remember no exception'). Note however that Breton 1667 (17th-c. Island Carib) treats accent/quantity as lexically marked with no general rule ('Difficilement pourra-t-on faire des regles generales & certaines pour les accents', 1877 ed. p. 6), and Taylor 1938's stress-marked Dominican vocabulary (BAE Bull. 119: 152-159) shows penult as well as antepenult stress in trisyllables (kuno'bu, bara'na vs. ya'wahu, mé'keru), so Rat's exceptionless rule may reflect the terminal, patois-dominant stage of the language or his limited corpus.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated words / citation forms as elicited; accent marked orthographically on each word; no discussion of phrase-level prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Rat 1898 and Taylor 1938 describe the terminal stage of Island Carib proper in Dominica (isla1278, ISO crb), recorded from last speakers/rememberers in the 1890s and 1930s; Breton 1667 describes 17th-c. Dominican Island Carib (same glottocode). The Stanford Phonology Archive 'Island Carib' entry (and Taylor 1951/1955/1956-58 IJAL 'Island Carib' papers listed by Glottolog under isla1278) actually describe the Central American (Hopkins, Belize) dialect, i.e. Garifuna (gari1256), whose stress ('not predictable', mostly second syllable in 3+-syllable words) differs from Rat's Dominican antepenult rule and should not be attributed to isla1278.

sources.note: 'Language and vocabulary' pp. 152-159: 'Stress is denoted by the apostrophe, as in supplemen'tary' (p. 152); every vocabulary item is stress-marked but no rule is stated. Marks show both antepenult (ya'wahu, mé'keru, ka'buru, kara'bali) and penult (kuno'bu, bara'na, kariphu'né) stress in polysyllables from 1930s rememberers.

sources.citation: Breton, Raymond. 1667 [reprint 1877, ed. L. Adam & Ch. Leclerc]. Grammaire caraïbe. Paris: Maisonneuve.
sources.note: 'De l'Accent, où Quantité', 1877 ed. p. 6 (=1667 p. 15): three kinds of 'accent' (short-acute, long-acute, extra-long for superlatives), marked lexically with acute accents; 'Difficilement pourra-t-on faire des regles generales & certaines pour les accents' — i.e. no general rule, accent/length must be learned word by word. Adam's 1877 grammatical introduction says nothing on accent.
